analysis.one_liner: Bans the IRS from offering free tax filing except through industry-run programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 112 cosponsors from both parties but never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the IRS from ever building or offering free tax preparation and filing directly to taxpayers, allowing free filing only through the industry-run Free File program and a few limited IRS assistance programs. It would also repeal a 1998 law that directs the Treasury Department to develop a 'return-free' tax system — a system, used in many other countries, in which the government sends you a pre-filled return to check and sign. In short, it would lock in commercial tax preparers and software companies as the only way most people could file for free.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial tax preparation and software companies. The bill would make their Free File program the only free electronic filing channel and would eliminate the legal mandate to study return-free filing, preserving the market for paid preparation and software.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the IRS from developing or providing free individual tax electronic preparation and filing services except through the Free File program and a few limited IRS assistance programs, keeping private companies as the gatekeepers of free filing.

It would repeal Section 2004 of the 1998 IRS Restructuring and Reform Act, which directs the Treasury Secretary to develop a return-free tax system — the legal path toward pre-filled government returns.
The bill took effect on enactment and carried no offsetting consumer protections, according to the introduced text.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary taxpayers, especially the roughly 150 million individual filers with simple returns, who would continue to spend hours on paperwork or pay a preparer or software company each year, with no government-run free alternative and no return-free option ever developed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Every individual taxpayer filing each year

drawbacks.text: Taxpayers would remain dependent on the Free File program and commercial preparers for filing help, and the only statutory path toward a simpler return-free system would be wiped out.

A good-faith objection: government-run free filing or pre-filled returns could make the government both tax collector and filing service, raising conflict-of-interest concerns; supporters of the bill framed Free File and private options as preserving 'choice' for taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main effect runs to a concentrated industry: it would permanently entrench commercial tax software and preparation companies in the filing process and kill the statutory path to return-free filing. The benefit to ordinary people is limited to keeping the existing private options; the cost is continued paperwork or annual fees and the loss of a simpler alternative that many countries already use. Weighing honestly, this bill serves the industry's business model far more than it serves filers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Melissa Hart introduced the bill on April 6, 2006, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
112 members cosponsored the bill — 94 Republicans and 18 Democrats.
The committee took no further action: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead because the bill died: the 1998 law directing Treasury to develop return-free filing stays on the books, and industry-run Free File did not become the legally protected only free channel. Tax preparation companies failed to codify their position, though they retained the status quo in practice.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary filers; the industry's plan died

for.name: Rep. Melissa Hart
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 111 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 18 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Eshoo, Lofgren, Crowley, Honda, and Capuano.

for.name: Tax preparation and software industry
for.role: Industry whose Free File program and paid products the bill protects
for.what_they_did: Its 2002 agreement with the IRS made Free File the existing free-filing channel, and the industry has long opposed a government-run return-free filing system; this bill would have codified that arrangement.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship skewed heavily Republican — 94 of 232 Republicans versus 18 of 202 Democrats — though the bill had genuine bipartisan sponsorship; no roll-call vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and software companies (Intuit, H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt and others)
industries.note: The bill would make the industry-run Free File program the only free electronic filing channel and repeal the return-free mandate, locking companies into the gatekeeper role for free filing and preserving demand for paid preparation and software. Its gain is the public's cost: taxpayers would keep paying for a service a return-free system could largely eliminate.

industries.industry: Paid tax preparers and seasonal filing services
industries.note: By blocking return-free filing, the bill protects the market for paid preparation, which ordinary filers bear as annual fees or hours of paperwork.
